headline: Rates Inch Lower as Stock Selloff Pulls Yields Down
tileReason: The daily 30-year average dipped to 7.45% Thursday, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5% this morning as investors left stocks for the safety of bonds.
takeaway:
Rates dipped again Thursday, but only a hair. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average slipped to 7.45% from 7.46% Wednesday, the third small improvement in a row and the smallest of the three. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, released Thursday, jumped to 7.28% from 7.11% because it caught up with the run-up in rates earlier this month.

A stock selloff did the heavy lifting. Stocks fell about 2% Thursday, a sixth straight losing day for the S&P 500, as worries about the money being poured into artificial intelligence deepened and Anthropic's stock market debut failed to lift the mood. When investors sell stocks they often buy Treasury bonds for safety, and the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, ended Thursday near 5.05%, down from about 5.07%.

Lenders passed along only a little of it. Mortgage News Daily noted that bonds were slightly weaker early Thursday and only improved after stocks slid around mid-morning, so most lenders had already set their rates for the day. That's why the daily average moved just 0.01%.

The bond rally picked up overnight. Stock futures fell again this morning, oil eased about 1%, and the 10-year yield dropped to roughly 4.98%, its first move below 5% in more than a week. A final University of Michigan survey released at 7 AM PT showed consumers expect less inflation over the next year (3.7%, down from 4.3% in the early-November reading), which also helps. Mortgage bond prices rose Thursday; an updated reading for this morning wasn't available. Today's daily index posts this afternoon.

A December Fed hike is still expected. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 90% to 94% as of Thursday afternoon and evening, with the rest on a bigger half-point move after Governor Waller said this week the Fed may need to act forcefully. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast. Waller and Governor Cook both speak today.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff, and it leaves room for rates to improve if bonds keep rallying.

The next tests come quickly. The Fed's preferred inflation measure (PCE, a broad gauge of consumer prices) is due Wednesday, Nov 25, just before Thanksgiving, when bond markets close. After that: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stock selloff sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Stocks fell about 2% Thursday, the S&P 500's sixth straight loss, on worries about AI spending, and futures fell again this morning. Investors moving money from stocks into Treasury bonds pushes bond prices up and yields down, and the 10-year yield slipped below 5% this morning.

drivers.title: Fed officials expect more hikes
drivers.text: A December hike is all but fully expected, October meeting minutes showed almost all officials see more increases ahead, and Governor Waller has raised the idea of a bigger half-point step. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row and wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Oil and inflation expectations easing
drivers.text: Oil is on track for a third weekly decline and slipped about 1% more this morning, and consumers in the University of Michigan survey now expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.3% earlier this month. Cooler inflation worries help bond prices and can pull yields lower.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields, and have room to lower rates if bonds keep rallying.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 19 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even. Mortgage rates have eased three days in a row to about 7.45%, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5% this morning as investors fled a stock selloff. In borrowers' favor: falling stocks, easing oil and lower inflation expectations, plus mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is almost fully expected, officials talk of more increases, and inflation reports keep running hot, so a rebound in stocks or a hot report could reverse the bond rally quickly. Big swing events: the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average eased to 7.45% Thursday, the third small dip in a row, and bond yields fell further this morning. Still, the Fed is expected to raise its short-term rate in December, so the next few weeks could be bumpy. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are holding near 7.45%, and Freddie Mac's weekly average jumped to 7.28%, so buyers are feeling the pinch heading into the holidays. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates eased slightly to about 7.45% as a stock selloff pushed bond yields lower, but a December Fed hike is still expected.
